identified_claims.claim_text: Specific heuristic modifications (allowing nouns for pronouns, skipping determiners/adjectives/adverbs, weighting trigram score by number-of-digits^10, and post-processing with bigram scoring) significantly improve sentence encoder performance.
evidence: Section 3.4 lists the four heuristic changes and states they 'greatly improve its performance.'
Qualitative examples in Section 4 illustrate improved compactness and plausibility.
uncertainty_flags: No ablation experiments isolate or quantify each heuristic's contribution or justify the exponent=10 choice.
Term 'greatly improve' is qualitative; lacking objective metrics (length distributions, human plausibility scores, or memorability by heuristic ablation).

identified_claims.claim_text: The sentence encoder can be used in practice to help memorize short numeric secrets and could improve security practices by enabling stronger passcodes through mnemonic assistance.
evidence: Intro and conclusions discuss use-cases (phone passcodes, account numbers, digits of π) and claim the encoder helps memorize numbers.
User study framed as password memorability with subjective preference favoring sentence encodings.
uncertainty_flags: Security implications (entropy preservation, attacker models, leakage from predictable templates/words) are not measured or modeled.
Real-world adoption, user behavior, and resistance to attacker inference are speculative beyond the experimental setting.

strengths.title: Clear engineering pipeline with concrete heuristics
strengths.description: The paper specifies a reproducible pipeline combining POS templates and n-gram scoring, with concrete implementation details (vocabulary intersection, trigram LM, template filtering, and four heuristics).
evidence: Section 3.1 (data sets), 3.3 (models), and 3.4 (complete description of sentence encoder and heuristics).
Examples in Section 4 and promised code release.

strengths.title: Focused empirical user study targeting memorability
strengths.description: Authors designed and ran an online two-wave study to evaluate short-term recall, 7-day recall, recognition, and subjective ease — metrics closely aligned with the stated research question.
evidence: Section 5 describes study design, timing, tasks, and outcome metrics; results reported in 5.3.
Reported statistically significant short-term recall and confirmation-time differences favoring sentence encoder.

strengths.title: Thorough presentation of comparative model variants
strengths.description: The manuscript explores a reasonable design space (Random, Unigram, n-gram, POS, Chunk, Sentence) and explains trade-offs qualitatively, aiding reproducibility and interpretability.
evidence: Sections 3.2 and 3.3 detail baselines and preliminary models; Section 4 compares outputs and discusses chunking, length, and running time trade-offs.

concerns.title: High participant exclusion and potential sample bias
concerns.description: A large fraction of initially collected participants (101 of 167) were excluded as 'fraudulent', leaving only 66 valid participants; this raises concerns about selection bias, reduced power, and robustness of reported p-values.
evidence: Section 5.1: 167 completed both surveys; 101 flagged due to suspicious timing, grouped emails, and perfect recall; final n=66 after exclusion.
Shared analysis flags this as a key uncertainty and recommends sensitivity checks.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide detailed logs and sensitivity analyses: (a) exact exclusion criteria and thresholds; (b) summary stats (demographics, timestamps) for excluded vs included participants; (c) re-run analyses under alternative exclusion thresholds and with excluded cases included to assess robustness; (d) report exact confidence intervals for reported proportions and effect sizes.

concerns.title: Missing ablation and sensitivity analyses for core heuristics
concerns.description: Key design choices (e.g., digit-weight exponent = 10, number of templates = 100, POS skip rules) are asserted to 'greatly improve' performance but lack controlled ablation experiments to quantify their individual impact on output plausibility, length, and memorability.
evidence: Section 3.4 lists four changes and claims improved performance but no ablation data presented; shared analysis calls for isolated tests.
Uncertainty flags explicitly note lack of ablation for exponent and template count.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run ablation experiments: systematically toggle each heuristic and measure changes in (a) average number of words per encoded digit, (b) LM likelihood/perplexity and human-rated grammaticality for a sample, and (c) memorability in a smaller controlled user study or online pilot. Report sensitivity to exponent values (e.g., 0, 2, 5, 10, 20).

concerns.title: Inadequate controls on the short-term distraction task
concerns.description: The intended distraction duration (~5 minutes) was not enforced; observed median time for non-fraud participants was 81 seconds, undermining the short-term recall manipulation and potentially inflating recall rates.
evidence: Section 5.2 states reading recipes for approx five minutes; Section 6 and shared analysis note realized average ~81 seconds.
Shared analysis flags this as affecting short-term recall validity.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: In revisions, report distribution of distraction times, enforce fixed minimum distraction time in future runs (e.g., timer), and re-run or replicate short-term recall with enforced distraction to verify effects persist.

concerns.title: Limited baseline coverage in human-subject comparisons
concerns.description: The user study compared only the n-gram baseline and the Sentence Encoder (plus raw numeric strings). Other variants (POS, chunk, unigram/random) were not tested with humans, leaving the relative performance landscape incompletely evaluated.
evidence: Sections 3 and 5 show multiple encoder variants but Section 5 study only assigned participants to n-gram or sentence groups.
Shared analysis recommends broader baseline inclusion to contextualize gains.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Either include additional encoder variants in the user study or justify and empirically demonstrate why n-gram is the most relevant baseline (e.g., preliminary automated metrics showing POS/chunk are close to sentence and infeasible to test).

concerns.title: Statistical reporting lacks robustness checks
concerns.description: Statistical tests (z-tests, t-tests) are reported without confidence intervals, effect sizes, or verification of assumptions given small n after exclusions.
evidence: Section 5.3 lists p-values and test names but does not report confidence intervals or exact effect sizes; shared analysis flags possible test assumption violations.
Sample counts (e.g., 29/31 vs 26/36) are small enough that exact binomial or Fisher tests and CIs would be informative.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report exact counts with 95% CIs, use Fisher's exact test or exact binomial tests where appropriate, report effect sizes (risk difference, odds ratio) and adjusted p-values for multiple comparisons; include power analysis.

concerns.title: Coverage and failure-mode analysis missing for arbitrary-length encoding claim
concerns.description: The manuscript claims the encoder can 'encode all numbers' and scales to long sequences (e.g., π) but provides only illustrative examples without systematic failure-rate, runtime, or vocabulary-constraint analyses.
evidence: Section 3.4 asserts full encodability; Section 4 provides examples for 8-digit and 50-digit inputs; no failure rate or runtime stats shown.
Shared analysis flags the vocabulary intersection (~34k words) and template filters as potential constraints requiring testing.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide empirical coverage statistics across many random sequences and lengths (e.g., percent successfully encoded within N template samples), distribution of sentence lengths, and encoding runtime. Report any cases requiring fallback or failing to find a template and describe limits.

concerns.title: Overstated claims around security/usability benefits
concerns.description: The suggestion that the system could improve security practices (by enabling stronger passcodes) is speculative without analysis of entropy preservation, predictability, or attacker models.
evidence: Intro and conclusion suggest security benefits; no empirical or theoretical analysis of entropy leakage or attacker exploitation of common templates/words.
Shared analysis recommends computing entropy preservation and attacker models.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Either temper claims about security benefits or add an analysis estimating entropy preserved by mapping digits to sentences, and discuss attacker scenarios (e.g., if users adopt template-based mnemonics, do common words reduce effective password entropy?).

comparable_works.relevance: Related corpus-based mnemonic generation (encoding bits as memorable word sequences); contrasts in that their methods did not make decoding back to original bits easy, while this paper ensures decodability via the major system.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similar goal (memorable encodings) and corpus methods, but different encoding constraints (bits vs digits) and different decoding affordances (Gh. & K. prioritized memorability; current paper prioritized decodability via major system).

comparable_works.relevance: Prior corpus-based mnemonic approach (headline-first-letter mapping), showing limited coverage; motivates need for generation rather than retrieval.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Shared objective of deriving memorable prompts from corpora; current paper uses generation from templates rather than retrieving headlines, improving coverage and controllability.

comparable_works.relevance: Informs experimental design for password memorability and multi-wave testing; provides precedent that mnemonic-based passphrases can be memorable.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Methodological precedent for multi-wave study but does not address constrained encoding requirements of the major system.

uncertainty_flags: Large participant exclusion (101/167) may introduce selection bias and reduce effective statistical power.
Key heuristic choices (digit-weight exponent, number of templates, POS-skip rules) lack ablation or principled justification.
Short-term distraction timing was shorter than intended (median 81s) and not enforced, weakening the validity of short-term recall outcome.
Long-term free-recall did not differ across groups; positive long-term signals are recognition and subjective ratings which have different implications than free recall.
Vocabulary restricted to Brown ∩ CMU (~34k words) and templates from Brown corpus may limit naturalness and cross-cultural generality; no tests on other corpora or demographics.
alternative_interpretations: Observed short-term recall advantage might stem from the sentence outputs being shorter/fewer words (compactness) rather than syntactic plausibility per se; weighting exponent favors words encoding many digits and could be the main driver.

Selection/exclusion process may have removed low-quality participants who would have failed differently across conditions, inflating apparent effects; excluded participants reportedly had perfect recall suggesting non-random exclusion.

Recognition advantages could reflect familiarity-based cues (distinctive words) or elimination strategies rather than true decoded-free recall improvements; recognition tasks are known to overestimate usable memory.
The n-gram baseline may have been an especially weak comparator because it tends to produce longer incoherent outputs; some other baseline (POS or chunk) might reduce or eliminate the gap.
transparency_notes: The manuscript promises code release but URL was withheld for blind review; releasing code and generation logs (templates tried, timeouts, candidate lists) would enable reproduction and independent ablation.

Exclusion criteria for fraudulent participants are described qualitatively; providing exact heuristics and per-participant metadata (timestamps, durations, hashed emails) under privacy constraints would improve auditability.
Statistical results are reported with p-values and test types but without confidence intervals, exact effect sizes, or multiple-comparison corrections; adding these would increase transparency.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The approach of combining POS-template sampling with an n-gram LM under a decoding constraint (major system) appears uncommon in the surveyed prior work within the manuscript; novelty is plausible. However, novelty alone does not guarantee empirical validity—robust validation (ablations, broader baselines, stronger human-subject controls) is required to confirm impact.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If ablations show the digit-weighting and POS-template sampling indeed drive compactness and plausibility, then the method's memorability gains are likely robust.
If wider sampling of templates (or other corpora) preserves plausibility and coverage, approach generalizes across user populations and input lengths.

If replication with stricter distraction timing and a larger, audited participant pool reproduces short-term and recognition improvements and shows long-term free-recall benefits for longer sequences, practical utility for passcodes is supported.

If entropy analyses show that sentence encodings do not substantially reduce effective entropy compared to raw digits (or if risk can be mitigated by per-user template randomization), security claims hold more weight.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Combines established components (POS templates, n-gram LM, major-system mapping) with pragmatic heuristics to create a usable encoder. The integration and concrete heuristics make it a useful engineering contribution though not radically novel in fundamental techniques.
evidence: Sections 3.3-3.4 detail how prior elements are combined and adapted with heuristics.
Prior work cited (Ghazvininejad & Knight, Jeyaraman & Topkara) covers related goals but not this exact constrained-generation approach.
uncertainty_flags: Absence of ablation leaves open whether novelty is in integration or in specific heuristic tuning; further experiments needed.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Human-subjects evidence shows positive signals (short-term recall, recognition, subjective preference) for the sentence encoder vs an n-gram baseline. However, high exclusion rates, insufficient controls on distraction timing, lack of baseline breadth, and missing robustness checks temper confidence in empirical generalization.
evidence: Section 5.3 reported statistically significant short-term recall and time differences; long-term recognition and subjective preference data also reported.
Shared analysis documents methodological weaknesses affecting inference.
uncertainty_flags: Sample validity and lack of ablations create substantial uncertainty about the reproducibility and generalizability of the empirical results.

novelty_lenses.rationale: If validated and extended (robust ablations, coverage guarantees, security analysis), the method could meaningfully influence how mnemonic encoders are constructed for security/usability. In its current state, lacking rigorous validation and security analysis, disruption is limited to practical prototypes and user tools rather than immediate paradigm shifts.
evidence: Concrete encoder capable of producing human-readable encodings and examples for long sequences (π) indicate potential.
Absence of attacker modeling and entropy analyses restrain security-relevant adoption.
uncertainty_flags: Success depends on follow-up experiments and security analyses; novelty in application rather than technique.

confidence_interval.rationale: I am moderately confident (central mass) that the Sentence Encoder design produces qualitatively more compact and syntactically structured encodings than naive baselines (supported by examples and model description). I am less confident that the human-subject results robustly generalize due to large exclusions, lack of ablation, and issues with the distraction manipulation. Therefore the interval reflects strong belief in the engineering plausibility but substantial uncertainty about empirical robustness and generalizability.

consensus_findings: The paper proposes a concrete, reproducible engineering pipeline (the 'sentence encoder') that samples POS sentence templates and fills slots with an n-gram LM augmented by heuristics to produce mnemonic sentences that are decodable under the major system.
Qualitative outputs and examples indicate the sentence encoder tends to produce shorter, more sentence-like and distinctive encodings compared to simpler greedy or plain n-gram outputs.

An online human-subjects study (after exclusions) reports evidence that sentence encodings outperform an n-gram baseline on some measures: short-term recall, faster confirmation times, recognition, and subjective ease ratings. Free long-term recall after one week did not show statistically significant differences.

Major methodological gaps exist that limit causal attribution and generalization: (a) no ablation/sensitivity analyses isolating heuristic contributions (e.g., digit-weight exponent, POS-skip rules); (b) high participant exclusion rate (101/167) and limited disclosure of exclusion procedures; (c) distraction task timing deviated from intended design (median ~81s vs intended ~5min); and (d) only one baseline (n-gram) was tested in the human study while other algorithmic variants were evaluated qualitatively.
disagreements: Degree of novelty: reviewers agree the engineering integration is meaningful but differ on magnitude — some view the combination as a modest incremental engineering contribution, others see a clearer novelty signal because directly comparable reversible digit-to-sentence systems are sparse.

Interpretation of empirical strength: reviewers agree on observed short-term/recognition signals but disagree about how convincing they are given the exclusions and missing robustness checks (some treat the results as promising but preliminary; others emphasize the need for replication and additional analyses before drawing substantive conclusions).

Root cause of memorability gains: one perspective attributes gains to syntactic plausibility from template sampling, while others propose an alternative explanation that gains may primarily come from compressing digits into fewer words (digit-weighting), i.e., reduced load rather than syntax per se.

Scope of coverage/scalability claim: some reviewers accept the provided examples (e.g., 50 digits of pi) as reasonable demonstration of scalability potential; others insist the 'encode all numbers' claim is unsupported without systematic failure-rate and runtime data.
uncertainty_hotspots: Heuristic ablations and sensitivity: impact and justification of the four core heuristics (noun-for-pronoun, POS skipping, digit-weight exponent=10, bigram post-processing) are unquantified and could materially change outputs and memorability.

Participant-exclusion procedure and sample representativeness: 101 exclusions (out of 167) materially reduce sample size; uncertainty about whether exclusion heuristics were appropriate, whether exclusions biased results, and how sensitive outcomes are to alternate thresholds.

Short-term distraction validity: intended ~5-minute distraction was not enforced (median ~81s), raising uncertainty about the short-term recall measure and whether it validly captures short-term memory decay.

Statistical inference robustness: p-values are reported but confidence intervals, effect sizes, exact-test alternatives (binomial/Fisher) and checks of test assumptions are missing; small effective n heightens uncertainty.

Coverage and runtime for long sequences: lack of large-scale automatic testing means unknown failure rates, average words-per-digit scaling, and runtime behavior when encoding very long sequences or adversarial digit patterns.
Security/entropy implications: absence of attacker-model analysis or entropy estimates leaves uncertain whether sentence encodings preserve effective secrecy or introduce exploitable structure.
model_diversity_effects: Including multiple encoder designs (random, unigram, n-gram, POS, chunk, sentence) in the manuscript clarifies a design space and highlights trade-offs (length vs plausibility vs runtime), but only one comparator (n-gram) was evaluated with humans; this limited cross-model sampling inflates uncertainty about how much benefit is unique to the sentence encoder versus achievable by other structured variants.

Heuristic-driven model diversity (varying POS relaxations, digit-weighting) likely changes sentence length and word distinctiveness; if gains are driven mainly by compression, then different models that prioritize words encoding more digits (even without POS templates) could perform similarly. Thus, model diversity both suggests alternative practical solutions and implies effects may be sensitive to specific design choices.

Corpus and vocabulary choices (Brown corpus + CMUdict intersection) impose a particular linguistic prior; alternative corpora or expanded vocabularies might shift which templates are frequent and which words are selected, potentially affecting memorability across populations—i.e., diversity in training data will likely change both linguistic plausibility and recognizability of outputs.
meta_review.editor_guidance: Center editorial decisions on the paper's transparency and verifiability rather than a single accept/reject judgment. The manuscript contributes a clear engineering pipeline and promising empirical signals, but the strength of empirical claims depends on additional analyses. Request revisions that: (1) provide full disclosure of participant-exclusion heuristics and anonymized summary logs plus a sensitivity analysis showing how primary outcomes change under alternative exclusion thresholds; (2) add ablation and sensitivity experiments for the main heuristics (digit-weight exponent, POS-skip rules, template count) with automated plausibility metrics and at least small-scale human plausibility checks; (3) recompute primary statistical tests with exact/binomial/Fisher alternatives, include 95% confidence intervals and effect sizes, and report contingency tables; (4) present large-scale automatic coverage/failure-rate and runtime experiments across digit lengths (e.g., 8, 50, 500 digits); and (5) temper or augment security-related claims with an entropy/attacker-model analysis or explicit limitations. Keep the editor as the decision-maker: these revisions will materially reduce current epistemic uncertainties and enable a clearer assessment of novelty and practical impact.
meta_review.author_guidance: Address key methodological weaknesses to substantiate claims. Concretely: (1) Share exact fraud-detection rules and per-participant timing summaries (anonymized). Run sensitivity analyses including alternate exclusion thresholds and report whether core results (short-term recall, recognition, subjective ratings, time-to-confirm) remain robust. (2) Perform ablation experiments toggling each heuristic and varying the digit-weight exponent (e.g., 1, 2, 5, 10, 20) and report effects on words-per-digit, LM scores/perplexity, and a sample of human grammaticality/fluency ratings; for the most impactful heuristics, include a small pilot memorability check. (3) Recompute statistical comparisons using exact tests where appropriate, provide contingency tables, 95% confidence intervals, and standardized effect-size measures. (4) Produce a large-scale automatic evaluation of coverage and runtime: attempt encoding of many random digit sequences at multiple lengths, report success/failure rates, distribution of sentence lengths, and time per digit. (5) Either add a concise entropy/attacker-model analysis (estimating how much information is leaked by the mapping and whether common templates/words create attacker priors) or explicitly limit security claims. (6) Add quantitative linguistic-plausibility metrics (perplexity under an external LM, human grammaticality ratings) for a representative sample of outputs and baselines. Finally, make code, template lists, and generation logs available for reproducibility.
transparency_report: All reviewers noted the manuscript promises code release but the submission lacks ablation logs, per-participant exclusion logs, and large-scale coverage/runtime data needed for independent verification.
The participant-exclusion procedure was described but not fully enumerated with thresholds or per-subject metadata; this reduces reproducibility and auditability of study results.
Statistical reporting presently omits confidence intervals, contingency tables, effect sizes, and checks of test assumptions; reanalysis with exact tests and CIs is required for transparency.
Hyperparameter choices (e.g., digit-weight exponent=10, 100 templates) are reported but not justified or surfaced with sensitivity runs; hyperparameter search artifacts and seeds are not provided.
Qualitative claims about syntactic plausibility and 'greatly improved performance' lack quantitative backup (perplexity/human ratings) and so transparency about linguistic evaluation is incomplete.
epistemic_limits: Current evidence supports the engineering plausibility of the sentence-encoder approach and provides preliminary human-subjects signals, but there remain substantial epistemic limits preventing strong, general conclusions. Limitations include: (1) inability to attribute memorability gains to specific design components without ablation; (2) uncertainty about the representativeness of the participant sample after large exclusions and potential sensitivity of results to inclusion thresholds; (3) incomplete validation of the short-term recall manipulation due to non-enforced distraction timing; (4) lack of systematic coverage/failure-rate and runtime data for long or adversarial digit sequences; and (5) absence of entropy/attacker-model analyses necessary to evaluate practical security implications. These limits imply that while the core idea is promising, claims about generalizability, scalability to arbitrary lengths, and security benefit remain provisional until the recommended analyses are completed.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: This manuscript presents an engineering pipeline (the "sentence encoder") that generates mnemonic sentences for numeric sequences under the major system by sampling frequent POS sentence templates (from the Brown corpus), filling slots using a trigram n-gram language model constrained to words in the Brown ∩ CMU Pronouncing Dictionary vocabulary, and applying four heuristics (noun-for-pronoun substitution, skipping some POS, weighting word scores by digits-encoded^10, and bigram post-processing). Qualitative examples show shorter, more sentence-like outputs vs simpler encoders. An online two-wave human-subjects study (after excluding many suspected fraudulent responses) compares the sentence encoder to an n-gram baseline and raw numeric strings on short-term recall, 7-day free recall, recognition, and subjective ease; reported results show statistically significant short-term recall and faster confirmation time favoring the sentence encoder, plus recognition and subjective-preference signals, while 7-day free recall shows no significant difference. Reviewers converge that the engineering idea is plausible and potentially useful but that methodological gaps (participant exclusions, missing ablations/sensitivity analyses, limited baseline coverage, distraction timing deviation, lack of coverage/runtime metrics, and absent security/entropy analysis) materially limit the strength and generalizability of empirical claims.
strengths: Clear, reproducible engineering pipeline: manuscript details corpus choices, vocabulary filtering (Brown ∩ CMUdict), template extraction, trigram scoring, and the four heuristics enabling replication.
Practical focus and motivating use-case: targeted evaluation for passcode-scale (8-digit) memorability with worked examples including longer sequences (50 digits of π).
Human-subjects evaluation aligned to memorability metrics: short-term recall, long-term recall, recognition, confirmation time, and subjective ease were measured and reported.

Exploration of design space: several encoder variants (random, unigram, n-gram, POS, chunk, sentence) are described and qualitatively compared, clarifying trade-offs (length vs plausibility vs runtime).
limitations: High participant-exclusion rate and incomplete transparency: 101 of 167 initial respondents were excluded as 'fraudulent' using heuristics described qualitatively; no anonymized per-participant summary logs, exclusion-by-rule counts, or sensitivity analyses are provided to show robustness of reported effects to alternative thresholds.

Missing ablation and sensitivity analyses for core heuristics: the four claimed heuristic improvements (noun-for-pronoun substitution, skipping determiners/adjectives/adverbs, digit-weight multiplier exponent = 10, and bigram post-processing) lack controlled ablation experiments or sensitivity sweeps (e.g., varying exponent), so causal attribution of memorability gains is unresolved.

Limited baseline coverage in human study: only the n-gram encoder (plus raw digits) was evaluated with participants; other described variants (POS, chunk, unigram, random) were only qualitatively compared, leaving open whether simpler or alternative structured encoders might yield similar memorability.

Short-term distraction duration not enforced: intended ~5 minute distraction was not realized (median ≈ 81 s for 'honest' participants), undermining interpretation of the short-term recall metric as reflecting comparable short-term-memory decay across participants.

Coverage and scalability claims under-supported: the assertion the encoder 'can encode all numbers' and scales arbitrarily is backed by examples (50 digits of π) but lacks systematic coverage/failure-rate statistics and runtime measurements across large random samples and longer lengths.

Security implications not evaluated: claims about practical security benefits (enabling stronger passcodes) are speculative without entropy-preservation estimates, attacker-model analyses, or evaluation of whether common templates/words create exploitable priors.
open_questions: Please provide anonymized summary logs of excluded participants (counts per exclusion rule, distributions of completion times, and basic demographics) and run sensitivity analyses showing how primary outcomes (short-term recall, recognition, subjective ratings) change under alternative exclusion thresholds.

Can the authors present ablation results toggling each of the four heuristics independently (and varying the digit-weight exponent across a range) reporting automated proxies (words-per-digit, LM score/perplexity) and a small-scale human plausibility/memorability check to quantify each heuristic's contribution?

Please supply systematic coverage experiments: attempt encoding large random samples of digit sequences at multiple lengths (e.g., 8, 50, 500 digits), report success/failure rates, average words-per-digit, and encoding runtime per digit; report fallback behavior when templates fail.

Recompute primary statistical tests using exact/binomial or Fisher approaches where appropriate, and report 95% confidence intervals and standardized effect sizes (risk differences, odds ratios, Cohen's d) plus contingency tables for all key comparisons.

If security claims remain, include an entropy/attacker-model analysis estimating how much information the sentence encoding leaks about original digits (mapping multiplicity, template/word frequency priors) or explicitly state limitations and avoidance of security claims.

Provide quantitative linguistic-plausibility metrics (e.g., perplexity under an external LM, human grammaticality/fluency ratings) for representative outputs from each encoder to support the 'syntactic plausibility' claim.
consensus_snapshot: The sentence encoder is a well-described, implementable engineering approach that produces shorter, more sentence-like mnemonic encodings for digit sequences in qualitative examples.
Human-subjects data provide preliminary evidence favoring the sentence encoder for short-term recall, confirmation speed, recognition, and subjective ease, but not for 7-day free recall.

Major methodological shortcomings (large exclusions, absent ablation/sensitivity analyses, limited baseline testing, non-enforced distraction duration, lack of coverage/runtime and security analyses) create substantive epistemic uncertainty about the generality and causal drivers of reported effects.
The combination of POS-template sampling plus digit-aware n-gram scoring is plausibly novel in this precise configuration and merits further validation rather than outright dismissal.
disagreement_snapshot: Reviewers differ on the magnitude of novelty: some view the work as a meaningful incremental engineering contribution (integration of known components), others regard the configuration as a clearer innovation signal because directly comparable reversible digit-to-sentence methods are sparse.

Interpretation of empirical strength: some reviewers consider the user-study signals promising despite limitations; others emphasize that the high exclusion rate and missing robustness checks substantially weaken confidence and call for replication.

On the causal mechanism of memorability gains: reviewers split between attributing gains to syntactic plausibility (POS templates) versus compression/shorter outputs driven by the digit-weight exponent favoring words encoding many digits.
uncertainty_snapshot: Heuristic dependence: unknown sensitivity of outputs and memorability to the digit-weight exponent and to template-count/selection; absent ablations create high uncertainty.
Sample representativeness: uncertainty whether exclusions removed fraudulent respondents only or also atypical but valid participants; lack of logs prevents adjudication.
Short-term recall validity: non-enforced distraction timing reduces confidence that the measured short-term effect reflects comparable cognitive decay across participants.
Scalability and failure modes: unknown rates of template exhaustion, rare-word selection, or runtime blow-ups for long/adversarial digit patterns.
Security impact: unknown whether sentence encodings preserve effective entropy or introduce predictable patterns an attacker could exploit.
source_trace: Manuscript Sections 3.1-3.4: description of Brown corpus, CMU Pronouncing Dictionary intersection (~34k words), POS-template selection (100 most frequent templates), trigram scoring, and the four heuristics (noun substitution, POS skipping, digits^10 weighting, bigram post-processing).
Manuscript Section 4 and Tables 2-3: qualitative examples of encodings (e.g., 'Officiate wasteland' for 86101521; 50 digits of π examples) and narrative comparison across encoder variants.

Manuscript Section 5 (Study Design & Results): two-wave online study protocol, participant exclusion counts (167 initial, 101 excluded), distraction task description (recipes), short-term recall and confirmation time results (29/31 vs 26/36; 27s vs 52s), long-term recognition and subjective preference results; reported p-values and test descriptions (z-test, t-test).

Shared analysis and specialist reviews: repeated flags regarding missing ablation/sensitivity analyses, high exclusion rate and need for anonymized logs, non-enforced distraction timing (median ~81s noted), absence of systematic coverage/runtime tests, and lack of entropy/attacker-model analysis (references to prior works Ghazvininejad & Knight 2015, Jeyaraman & Topkara 2005, Vu et al. 2004 appear in manuscript Section 2.2).
transparency_notes: Key transparency gaps identified by reviewers: (1) per-participant exclusion logs, exact exclusion rule thresholds, and anonymized timing/demographic summaries are missing and necessary to audit sample validity; (2) hyperparameter choices and any tuning logs (e.g., why exponent = 10, how 100 templates chosen) are reported but no sensitivity/ablation data are provided; (3) statistical reporting omits contingency tables, confidence intervals, and effect sizes—reanalysis with exact tests and CIs recommended; (4) no large-scale coverage/failure-rate or runtime experiments for long sequences are presented; (5) code release is promised but until released, independent reproduction and ablation are not possible.
human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: Request a revision focused on transparency and robustness before relying on the empirical claims for downstream decisions. Ask authors to: (A) publish anonymized exclusion summaries and perform sensitivity analyses demonstrating whether results hold under alternative exclusion thresholds; (B) add ablation/sensitivity experiments for the four heuristics (including varying the digit-weight exponent) with automated plausibility metrics and a small human pilot where feasible; (C) re-run or re-report statistical analyses with exact/binomial/Fisher tests, 95% confidence intervals, and effect sizes plus contingency tables; (D) provide large-scale automatic coverage and runtime results across varied digit lengths and random samples; and (E) temper security claims or include an entropy/attacker-model analysis. These revisions materially improve verifiability and clarify whether the reported memorability signals generalize.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen claims and address reviewers' concerns, provide the following in a revision: (1) Anonymized per-exclusion-rule counts and timing summaries (e.g., number excluded per rule, distribution of distraction times) and sensitivity analyses showing how primary outcomes change under alternate inclusion thresholds. (2) Ablation experiments toggling each heuristic independently and varying the digit-weight exponent (e.g., 1, 2, 5, 10, 20), reporting words-per-digit, LM likelihood/perplexity, and human-rated grammaticality/fluency for samples; for components with large offline effects, run a small pilot to measure memorability impact. (3) Statistical reanalysis: provide exact contingency tables for each comparison, use binomial/Fisher tests for proportions where appropriate, report two-sided 95% CIs and effect sizes (risk difference, odds ratio, Cohen's d), and discuss power. (4) Coverage and performance evaluation: attempt encoding of large random sets at multiple lengths (8, 50, 500 digits), report success/failure rates, average words-per-digit, and runtime per digit; describe fallback behaviors. (5) Either add a concise entropy/attacker-model analysis or explicitly limit claims about security benefits. (6) Release code, template lists, and generation logs (with seeds) and add a representative set of generated outputs used in the study to enable reproduction. Include quantitative linguistic-plausibility metrics (external LM perplexity or human judged grammaticality) to support the syntactic-plausibility claim.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
This manuscript introduces a practical sentence-encoder that combines POS-template sampling from the Brown corpus with a trigram LM and several heuristics to generate mnemonic sentences under the major system. Qualitative outputs are concise and sentence-like; a human study comparing the sentence encoder to an n-gram baseline shows significant short-term recall and confirmation-time advantages and recognition/subjective-preference signals, though 7-day free recall shows no advantage.

Strengths:
- Well-specified, reproducible engineering pipeline (data sources, vocabulary constraints, template selection, heuristics) enabling follow-up work.
- Practical user-facing motivation (passcode memorability) and aligned empirical metrics (short-term recall, long-term recall, recognition, subjective ease, timing).
- Clear comparative design space: authors explore multiple encoder variants and present illustrative outputs showing meaningful qualitative differences.

Limitations:
- Large participant-exclusion rate (101/167) with exclusion rules described but not audited; no anonymized logs or sensitivity analyses. This raises selection-bias and robustness concerns for reported p-values and effect sizes.
- No ablation or sensitivity analyses for the four central heuristics (including the digit-weight exponent = 10). Without these, it is unclear which components drive the reported memorability effects.
- Human study tested only the n-gram baseline (plus numeric strings); important encoder variants (POS, chunk, unigram) were not included in participant comparisons, limiting claims about superiority over the design space.
- The intended ~5-minute distraction period was not enforced (median ~81s for honest participants), undermining the interpretability of the short-term recall metric.
- Scalability/coverage claims ("encode all numbers") are supported by examples but lack systematic failure-rate and runtime statistics across random inputs and longer sequences.
- Security/usability implications (entropy leakage, attacker priors) are not analyzed; claims about improved passcode strength remain speculative.

Open Questions:
1) Please provide anonymized exclusion logs (counts per rule and timing summaries) and sensitivity analyses showing how key outcomes change if exclusion thresholds vary.
2) Can the authors run ablation experiments toggling each heuristic and varying the digit-weight exponent, reporting words-per-digit, LM scores/perplexity, and a small human plausibility/memorability pilot for the most impactful changes?
3) Please present coverage/failure-rate and runtime experiments on large random sets of digit sequences at multiple lengths (8, 50, 500 digits) and report fallback behavior and average sentence lengths.
4) Recompute statistical tests with exact/binomial/Fisher approaches where appropriate and include 95% confidence intervals, contingency tables, and effect-size measures for main comparisons.
5) If claiming security benefits, include an entropy/attacker-model analysis estimating leakage and guessing advantage from common templates/words, or else temper security claims.
6) Provide quantitative linguistic-plausibility metrics (external LM perplexity or human grammaticality/fluency ratings) for representative outputs across encoders.

Transparency:
Reviewers repeatedly requested releases or supplementary material that include (a) anonymized participant logs and exclusion breakdowns, (b) ablation/sensitivity experiment logs and seeds, (c) generation logs (templates tried, candidate lists), (d) contingency tables and CIs for all statistical tests, and (e) code plus template lists used to generate stimuli. The manuscript currently promises code release but does not provide these materials in-submission; releasing them will substantially reduce epistemic uncertainty.

confidence_interval.rationale: Upper bound justification: multiple reviewers found the engineering contribution and qualitative outputs credible and the human-study signals (short-term recall, recognition, subjective preference) supportive. Lower bound justification: pervasive methodological gaps (large exclusions without sensitivity analysis, missing ablations and coverage/runtime experiments, non-enforced distraction timing, limited baselines, and absent statistical robustness reporting) create substantial uncertainty about the generality and causal attribution of the empirical findings. The interval reflects moderate confidence in the core engineering idea but substantial uncertainty about empirical claims until requested analyses are provided.
